events_chronological: In the year the great war ended, the blind clockmaker Ferrier builds a station clock that runs backwards, in memory of the son it took from him.
On the night the war ends, the manufacturer Ellis Wray's wife dies in childbirth and he abandons the baby - an infant with the body of an old man - on the steps of a nursing home.
Odessa, who runs the home, takes Amos in and raises him among the elderly residents.
Amos, apparently in his eighties, gets out of his wheelchair and walks.
Amos meets six-year-old Clara, the granddaughter of a resident, and the two become inseparable.
Amos takes work on a tugboat skippered by a man called Rook and leaves the river city for the first time.
Wintering in a northern port, Amos has an affair with Eleanor Trask, the wife of a trade official.
The tug is drafted into the next war and Rook and most of the crew are killed ramming a submarine.
Amos comes home, and Ellis Wray reveals himself as his father and leaves him the fastener factory.
Clara, now a dancer in the capital, visits, and Amos turns her down as too young for him.
Clara's leg is shattered by a car abroad and she refuses Amos's help.
Her dancing over, Clara comes back to the river city, and she and Amos finally meet in the middle of their lives.
Odessa dies, and Amos and Clara sell up and live together on a boat and then in a house of their own.
Their daughter Josie is born, and Amos, visibly younger every year, decides she cannot have a father who will become her brother.
Amos signs everything over to Clara and leaves.
Clara marries again and raises Josie, while Amos travels the world alone and sends postcards.
Amos comes back once, in his twenties, and spends a night with Clara before leaving again.
Decades later Clara is called to collect a boy found in a derelict building with Amos's diary, and cares for him as he forgets everything.
Amos dies in Clara's arms as an infant.
With a hurricane bearing down on the coast, Josie finishes reading the diary to her dying mother and learns who her father was, while the backwards clock sits in a flooding storage room.
nonlinear_category_reason: The hospital room is the narrating frame, and the entire life after it is a diary read aloud in chronological order.
syuzhet_notes: This is a frame narrative rather than a shuffled one: told-order bullet 1 is the hospital room in the present, and everything after it is the contents of a diary read aloud in chronological order. The frame is not confined to the opening - it interrupts the diary repeatedly across the runtime, so the present-day material recurs where a single ordering can place it only once. What runs backwards in this film is the protagonist's body, not the telling.
fabula_notes: The protagonist ages in reverse, so his apparent age and his actual age move in opposite directions throughout; the ordering here follows chronological time rather than how old he looks. The years covered by the postcards are a montage, and the daughter's discovery of her parentage belongs to the frame's own present rather than to the diary.
